\section{Additional Results}\label{app:additional}
\setlength{\emergencystretch}{2em}% allow looser lines in the online appendix

This appendix collects results that support the main text but are not needed to follow it. Sections~\ref{app:add-chinchilla}
through \ref{app:add-flexible} follow the order of the paper: the canonical Chinchilla data, the technology across
sweeps, revealed inference demand, observational production functions, algorithmic progress, bias formulas for input
measurement and flexible inputs, and hyperparameters as flexible inputs. Section~\ref{app:add-claims} reports the verification register for the formal results.

\subsection{The Canonical Chinchilla Data}\label{app:add-chinchilla}

\emph{Exclusion rules.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-selection} shows how the Chinchilla estimates move as the $k$
highest-loss runs are dropped. The data exponent $\beta$ falls almost monotonically, from 0.453 with all 245 runs to
0.347 at $k=15$, while $\alpha$ stays between 0.345 and 0.349. The five runs that \citet{besiroglu2024chinchilla} drop
are the most data-starved runs of the $10^{19}$ IsoFLOP, with log residuals 9 to 45 times the residual standard
deviation. Their influence is leverage, not truncation bias: a truncated-Gaussian likelihood that conditions on the
exclusion rule reproduces the untruncated Gaussian estimates ($\beta=0.406$ in both), and dropping runs by their
data-to-parameter ratio instead of their loss gives the same answer. The revealed-preference verdict at
Chinchilla-70B depends on excluding these outliers but not on how: every rule that removes them yields $w$ between
0.95 and 1.06, whereas keeping them ($k\le2$) gives 1.24 or more and dropping the whole $10^{19}$ budget gives 0.78.

\emph{Duality.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-duality} reports the objects each of Chinchilla's three approaches estimates
and tests the cross-equation restrictions that link them (Proposition~\ref{prop:duality}). Tests must be
design-consistent: comparing the IsoFLOP argmins with the analytic Approach~3 path rejects even our own refit under
the stratified bootstrap, because parabola fits on a finite grid are biased \citep{czech2026problems}. Against the
design-consistent null, our refit and the \citet{besiroglu2024chinchilla} parameters are consistent with the argmins
($p\ge0.16$ in every classical or bootstrap-calibrated variant), whereas the published Approach~3 parameters of \citet{hoffmann2022training} are
marginally inconsistent ($p=0.040$ in the classical test and 0.060 with bootstrap calibration), mainly because their
implied compute-optimal model size at the center of the design is about 12 percent below the argmins. The frontier
restrictions are rejected for every technology under the stratified bootstrap (calibrated $p$ between 0.003 and 0.037)
but not under the wild bootstrap ($p\ge0.15$): the Approach~1 frontier through the minima lies 0.005 to 0.008 nats
below every Approach~3 frontier, a small lack of fit at the IsoFLOP minima.

\emph{Lab-own technologies.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-labs} applies the same comparison to the IsoFLOP experiments that
labs have published. Our Approach~2 fit reproduces Meta's Llama~3 law exactly, but the primal fitted to the same runs
implies a steeper path ($a=0.527$ against 0.463) in which $M^*$ falls rather than rises with compute. The difference
is significant at about the 5 percent level once the primal's own sampling error is included ($t=-2.1$) and not under
the wild bootstrap; the loss units of the digitized figure are unknown. For the Marin ladders the design-consistent
tests do not reject ($p$ between 0.33 and 0.54); about three-quarters of the naive discrepancy is finite-grid parabola
bias and the rest is FLOP accounting, because Marin's nominal budgets differ from $6ND$. The Marin exponents
($\alpha$ between 0.64 and 0.69) are far from Chinchilla's: exponents are specific to the recipe.

\subsection{The Technology across Sweeps}\label{app:add-tech}

\emph{Robustness.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-robust} reports the main estimates of Table~\ref{tab:technology} under
alternative parameter-count conventions, outputs, samples, and estimators. Conventions matter most for the allocation
exponent: counting Farseer's two untied embedding matrices moves $a$ from 0.526 to 0.411 (and $\sigma^*$ from 0.772 to
0.724), and dropping the two single-epoch runs in which \citet{muennighoff2023scaling} trained 1.1 and 2.8 billion
parameters on 100 million tokens moves $a$ from 0.535 to 0.360 and $M^*(10^{21})$ from 60 to 139. The output measure
also matters: with task bits per byte instead of C4 cross-entropy, the OLMo ladder's $\sigma^*$ falls from 0.825 to
0.763. Because $\sigma$ is ordinal, such differences reflect sampling noise and misspecification of the functional
form rather than the change of output units itself.

\emph{Neutrality of data quality.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-neutrality} nests the hypotheses about how better data enter.
Across the three web corpora of \citet{gadre2024language}, a Hicks-neutral scaling of reducible loss plus
corpus-specific asymptotes is not rejected ($p=0.90$) and explains 96.8 percent of the cross-corpus variation, but the
test has little power: the data- and parameter-augmenting alternatives are not rejected either. Across the 25
DataDecide recipes \citep{magnusson2025datadecide} every restriction is rejected, yet asymptote shifts alone explain
98.1 percent of the variation and a neutral scale brings this to 99.7 percent. The remaining factor bias is small in fit
but not in allocation: the recipe tilts $\ln(A_r/B_r)$ span 0.22 to 0.26, which implies compute-optimal ratios that
differ 2.9- to 3.4-fold across recipes and revealed wedges that differ by a factor of 1.25 to 1.29 at the same inputs.
The data-augmenting tilt belongs to the heavily filtered DCLM variants, which have the highest C4 asymptotes. Because
a data-augmenting tilt lowers $M^*$ by construction when exponents are common, and because quality is not measured
independently of the tilt, this pattern is not independent evidence on whether better data are data-augmenting.

\emph{Functional form on the best-designed sweep.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-farseer} compares the Chinchilla form with
richer forms on the Farseer grid of \citet{li2025predictableb}. The Chinchilla form extrapolates poorly in compute:
its out-of-sample error on the top decile of compute is 8 to 10 times that of Farseer's own nine-parameter form.
Figure~\ref{fig:app-farseer-sigma} shows the local elasticity of substitution estimated without any functional form.
Its median over the grid, 0.690, agrees with Farseer's form (0.706) and with the generalized family with a free outer
exponent (0.710), and lies below the Chinchilla-implied 0.77. Local $\sigma$ tends to fall with $D/N$ for the smallest
models, a pattern suggestive of stronger complementarity where over-trained models sit; it is not monotone at every
size, and the pointwise bands ignore smoothing bias.

\subsection{Revealed Inference Demand}\label{app:add-wedge}

\emph{Families.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-family} normalizes each family by its flagship. Smaller siblings are more
over-trained than their flagships in essentially every family: 95 percent of the 105 non-flagship siblings have
$w^{rel}>1$, and the exceptions are the five smaller Cerebras-GPT models, trained at a constant 20 tokens per
parameter. This pattern follows largely from the exponents once $D$ is given. The assumption that flagships are
training-optimal holds before 2024 (median flagship wedge 1.14; the 95 percent interval contains 1 for half of the 18
flagships) but fails afterward (median 3.14; the interval lies above 1 for 92 percent of 26 flagships), so
flagship-normalized demands are lower bounds for recent families. Meta is the exception: its flagships have $w=0.98$
under Meta's own IsoFLOP law. A single power-law demand for model size across families is rejected, but the test is
partly mechanical when $D$ is common within a family; among families whose token counts vary with size the rejection is
marginal ($p=0.047$) and disappears with flagship-normalized demand ($p=0.12$).

\emph{Rival explanations.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-rivals} evaluates alternatives to inference demand. Under-training
($w<1$), the signature of data scarcity or of Kaplan-era beliefs, disappears after 2023. Hardware tiers matter for
model sizes (26 percent of open models released since 2023 sit at 6.5 to 9.5 billion parameters, against 9 percent
under a log-normal benchmark) but only marginally for the wedge ($+0.11$ in logs, s.e.\ 0.06). A non-homothetic
technology can rationalize the token counts of the largest models but not those of the small ones: within Farseer's
support its Eq.~3 implies larger wedges than the Chinchilla form. Recipe-level factor bias of the size measured in
DataDecide cannot bring most models to $w\le1$. Table~\ref{tab:app-aggregate} reports the compute-weighted aggregate
by release year, and Table~\ref{tab:app-homothetic} shows how revealed $T/D$ for five prominent models depends on the
assumed compute-optimal ratio and curvature when $\alpha=\beta$.

\subsection{Observational Production Functions}\label{app:add-obs}

\emph{Other outputs and a cleaner sample.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-lalonde-robust} repeats the design-matched
comparison of Table~\ref{tab:lalonde} for two other benchmarks and for a sample without imputed token counts,
distilled, synthetic-data, or code models. The OLS bias in the compute elasticity is $-0.098$ (0.127) for ARC-Challenge
and $-0.160$ (0.102) for Winogrande, point estimates that imply 18 to 31 percent attenuation but are not significant; on
the cleaner HellaSwag sample it is $+0.045$ (0.023), significant under clustered normal inference but not under the
wild-cluster bootstrap ($p=0.10$). The parameter--data split is less stable: the sign of the $\theta_N$ bias changes
across outputs and estimators, and the family fixed-effects estimates, which rest on little within-family variation in
$D$, show large negative $\theta_D$ biases for every output.

\emph{Productivity dispersion.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-tfp} and Figure~\ref{fig:app-tfp-families} measure dispersion
in family productivity in compute-equivalent units. The 90/10 ratio across families is 23.7 (90 percent interval
$[9.1,197]$) for HellaSwag, falls to 18.3 without distilled and synthetic-data families and to 7.0 without code
families as well, and is 11.1 within developers, against 41 reported by \citet{mertens2026secret}. The synthetic-data
families Phi and SmolLM rank first and third of 38: when training data are generated by other models, measured
productivity includes the quality of those inputs, a gross-output problem. With returns to scale near one,
manufacturing's 90/10 ratio of 1.92 \citep{syverson2011determines} is also an input-equivalent ratio, so family
dispersion among language models is roughly three to five times larger in logs; expressed in reducible-loss units
(1.41 to 1.76) it looks similar to manufacturing, but that conversion is a choice of output units.

\subsection{Algorithmic Progress}\label{app:add-progress}

\emph{Replication.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-ho-replication} reproduces the preferred estimates of
\citet{ho2024algorithmic} exactly: objective, parameters, and the bootstrap median of the doubling time of effective
compute (8.44 months; the point estimate is 8.68). The published point is not the minimizer of the authors' own
objective: run to convergence, the same algorithm lowers the objective by 2 percent and moves the doubling time to 6.1
months with a paper-cluster interval of $[3.0,22.7]$. Almost all of that gain comes from the penalty on parameters
whose values depend on an arbitrary normalization; the fit improves by 0.3 percent. The point estimate therefore
depends on estimator choices (6.1 to 10.2 months) that the data cannot arbitrate, and the profile-likelihood interval
is $[4.1,40.5]$ months.

\emph{Why the cross-lab data elasticity is small.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-attenuation} decomposes the gap between the
cross-lab data exponent ($\hat\beta$ of 0.025 to 0.04) and experimental values near 0.37. Dropping the irreducible
loss is the key specification choice: on the Chinchilla sweep itself, the $E=0$ form collapses one exponent and lowers
the frontier elasticity from 0.178 to 0.053, the sample-mean elasticity of total rather than reducible loss. The
like-for-like gap between cross-lab estimates (0.021 to 0.027) and experiments is therefore about 2 to 2.5 times, not 7
to 9. Because dropping $E$ rescales exponents and year coefficients proportionally to first order, the progress rate
is much less affected than the exponents when the $E=0$ model is fitted to its global optimum (pseudo-true doubling
time 11.1 months against a true 12); the authors' procedure, however, can stop at a local optimum that overstates
progress (4.6 months when $D$ is measured as dataset size). How data are measured moves the estimate most: counting
effective data under repetition raises the doubling time to 25.7 months (12.7 with the authors' stopping rule). Within
the common-$E$ form, Ho et al.'s own data prefer $E=0$, so the case for this channel rests on the sweep and the Monte
Carlo.

\emph{Architecture gains and frontier regressions.}---Table~\ref{tab:app-ceg-sahal} shows that the data cannot tell
whether the compute-equivalent gain of transformers over other architectures depends on scale: the difference in
frontier elasticities is 0.008 $[-0.012,0.034]$ and the implied gains span six orders of magnitude. Regressions of loss
on compute without a time trend overstate the compute elasticity by a factor of 1.15 on all rows and 1.44 among
record-setting releases, within the range $\gamma/(1-s_A)$ predicts for algorithmic shares between 0.05 and 0.40.

\emph{Allocative versus technical progress.}---Figure~\ref{fig:app-allocative} decomposes the Kaplan-to-Chinchilla
rebalancing. Among models trained with at least $10^{23}$ FLOP, the geometric-mean Farrell cost efficiency rose by a
factor of 1.05 between 2020--21 and 2022--24 under the Besiroglu technology, 1.91 and 2.41 under the two versions of
Hoffmann's, and 1.58 under a Farseer fit: 2 to 40 percent of the gain implied by the Ho et al.\ rate over the same
interval. Across the other sweep technologies we estimate, the realized gain ranges from 0.55 to 4.3, and
Meta's own technology implies a loss (0.74), so even its sign depends on the technology. The 10-fold gain reported by
\citet{gundlach2025origin} is instead the counterfactual cost of continuing Kaplan's allocation rule, which reaches 5.2
at $3.8\times10^{25}$ FLOP and 11.7 at $5\times10^{26}$ FLOP under the Besiroglu technology.

\subsection{Bias Formulas for Input Measurement and Flexible Inputs}\label{app:add-biasformulas}

This subsection derives the two bias formulas used in Section~\ref{sec:tech:measurement}. Both were verified
symbolically and against brute-force IsoFLOP argmins.

\emph{Input measurement.}---Let the true technology be $L=E+AN^{-\alpha}+BD^{-\beta}$ and let the researcher count
$N_m$ parameters, where the true count is $N=N_m+X(N_m)$ and the omitted component has share $s\equiv X/N$ and a
constant scale elasticity $\theta\equiv d\ln X/d\ln N_m<1$. The researcher measures compute as $C_m=6N_mD$ and takes
the IsoFLOP argmin in measured units: $n_m\equiv\ln N_m$ minimizes $L$ subject to $\ln D=c_m-\ln6-n_m$, with
$c_m\equiv\ln C_m$. Because $d\ln N/dn_m=(N_m+\theta X)/N=1-s(1-\theta)\equiv\varphi$, the first-order condition is
$\alpha u\varphi=\beta v$, with $u=AN^{-\alpha}$ and $v=BD^{-\beta}$. Differentiating its log along the researcher's
path, with $d\ln u/dn_m=-\alpha\varphi$, $d\ln v=\beta\,(dn_m-dc_m)$ and $\zeta\equiv d\ln\varphi/dn_m$, gives
\[
(\zeta-\alpha\varphi)\,\frac{dn_m}{dc_m}=\beta\,\frac{dn_m}{dc_m}-\beta
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
a_m\equiv\frac{dn_m}{dc_m}=\frac{\beta}{\beta+\alpha\varphi-\zeta},
\]
which is equation~\eqref{eq:measbias}. With $\theta$ constant, $d\ln s/dn_m=\theta-\varphi$, so
$\zeta=(1-\theta)s(\varphi-\theta)/\varphi\ge0$, because $\varphi\ge\theta$. Since $\varphi\le1$ and $\zeta\ge0$, the
denominator is at most $\alpha+\beta$, and $a_m\ge a=\beta/(\alpha+\beta)$, with equality when $s=0$ or $\theta=1$. A
proportional error ($\theta=1$) gives $\varphi=1$ and $\zeta=0$ and moves only the level of the path. As $s\to1$,
$a_m\to\beta/(\beta+\alpha\theta)$, the small-scale limit of \citet{pearce2024reconciling}. The closed form matches
brute-force argmins to within $2\times10^{-7}$ in $\ln N$.

\emph{Flexible inputs.}---Let observed loss be $L_{\rm obs}=L^*e^{\iota(N,D)}$, where $L^*$ is the technology with
the hyperparameters concentrated out and $\iota\ge0$ is the inefficiency of the researcher's hyperparameter policy.
Along the IsoFLOP curve at compute $C$, write $f(n)$ for $L^*$ at $d=c-\ln6-n$, with minimizer $n^*(c)$; then
$f'=-\alpha u+\beta v$ and $f''=\alpha^2u+\beta^2v$, and at the minimizer $\alpha u=\beta v=\gamma R^*$, with $R^*$ the
reducible loss on the frontier, so $f''=(\alpha+\beta)\gamma R^*$. The observed argmin solves $f'(n)+\Delta(n)=0$,
where $\Delta\equiv\partial(L_{\rm obs}-L^*)/\partial n$ at fixed compute. Expanding around $n^*(c)$, the log argmin
shifts by $-\Delta(C)/f''(C)$ to first order in $\Delta$, and differentiating in $\ln C$ gives
$a_{\rm obs}-a=-\partial[\Delta/f'']/\partial\ln C$. At the minimizer $\Delta=L^*e^{\iota}(\iota_n-\iota_d)$, with
$\iota_n\equiv\partial\iota/\partial\ln N$ and $\iota_d\equiv\partial\iota/\partial\ln D$, so inefficiency that depends
on the inputs only through compute ($\iota_n=\iota_d$) leaves $a$ unbiased. With small, constant log-gradients,
$L^*=E+R^*$ and $R^*\propto C^{-\gamma}$ give $a_{\rm obs}-a=-(\iota_n-\iota_d)E/[(\alpha+\beta)R^*(C)]$. Under the
\citet{besiroglu2024chinchilla} technology the formula matches simulated IsoFLOP argmins to within 0.003 in $a$.

\subsection{Hyperparameters as Flexible Inputs}\label{app:add-flexible}

Table~\ref{tab:measurement} decomposes the Kaplan--Chinchilla discrepancy into input measurement and flexible inputs.
The tables below use the Step Law grid of \citet{li2025predictablea}, which trains every $(N,D)$ cell under many
learning rates and batch sizes, to study hyperparameters directly. Table~\ref{tab:app-steplaw} shows that this
17-cell design does not identify the allocation exponent: the likelihood is flat in $E$ while $a$ ranges from 0.76 to
0.45. Holding $E$ fixed, published hyperparameter rules shift $a$ by $-0.041$ to $+0.076$, all within 0.7
residual-bootstrap standard errors. Choosing one random configuration per cell costs mainly precision for $a$ (median
bias $-0.3$ standard errors) but biases $\sigma^*$ ($-0.051$, or $-3.7$ standard errors), so these data give no reason
to regard $\sigma^*$ as the more robust object. The stochastic frontier in Table~\ref{tab:app-sfa} shows that
inefficiency falls with training tokens ($\gamma_D$ between $-0.23$ and $-0.26$) but not significantly with
parameters: longer horizons flatten the loss surface in the hyperparameters. Because only the transverse gradient of
inefficiency biases the IsoFLOP exponent, this pattern implies a small downward bias ($-0.012$) for a researcher who
uses random configurations. Table~\ref{tab:app-demand} estimates the demand for the flexible inputs themselves. The
unconditional learning-rate demand replicates Step Law's; holding the batch fixed, the positive token elasticity
shrinks to between 0.02 and 0.05, but conditioning closes only 26 to 43 percent of the gap to the negative elasticity
reported by \citet{bjorck2024scaling}.

\subsection{Verification of the Formal Results}\label{app:add-claims}

Table~\ref{tab:app-claims} lists the formal statements of the paper with the checks applied to each. Every algebraic
identity was reduced to zero symbolically, and every comparative-static, bias, and information statement was also
checked by a method that does not use the closed form: brute-force optimization, simulation, or direct computation of
Fisher information. Three statements differ from formulations that are common in earlier drafts or readings of the
literature, and the paper uses the corrected versions: the sign of biased technical change is identified from the drift
of compute-optimal tokens per parameter, compute-equivalent gains are constant when the irreducible loss and the
frontier elasticity coincide (not the individual exponents), and forward and reverse regressions bracket the returns to
compute only when compute does not rise with productivity.
